original.title: An implicit inverse-trigonometric derivative
original.stem_html:
A curve is defined by

\[- 3 x + \sin{\left(2 y \right)}=0,\qquad -\frac13\lt x\lt \frac13,\quad -\frac\pi4\lt y\lt \frac\pi4.\]

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).
original.question_html:
A curve is defined by

\[- 3 x + \sin{\left(2 y \right)}=0,\qquad -\frac13\lt x\lt \frac13,\quad -\frac\pi4\lt y\lt \frac\pi4.\]

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to prove that

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2 p^{2} \tan{\left(2 y \right)}.\]
(b)[3]

Hence find the exact second derivative at \((\frac{1}{6},\frac{\pi}{12})\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate twice before using the original relation.

(b)

Evaluate the first derivative as well as the trigonometric factor.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[2 p \cos{\left(2 y \right)} - 3=0.\]

Differentiate once more:

\[- 4 p^{2} \sin{\left(2 y \right)} + 2 q \cos{\left(2 y \right)}=0.\]

Since \(\cos2y\ne0\) on the stated branch, divide by \(2\cos2y\) and rearrange:

\[q=2 p^{2} \tan{\left(2 y \right)}.\]

(b)

The first differentiated relation gives \(p=\sqrt{3}\). Substituting into the identity gives

\[q=2 \sqrt{3}.\]

original.title: Transforming a nonlinear equation through sine
original.stem_html:
A smooth function satisfies, on a neighbourhood of \(x=0\),

\[y^{\prime\prime}-\tan y\,(y^{\prime})^2+4y^{\prime}+4\tan y=e^{-x}\sec y,\]
\[y(0)=\frac\pi6,\qquad y^{\prime}(0)=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad -\frac\pi2\lt y\lt \frac\pi2.\]
original.question_html:
A smooth function satisfies, on a neighbourhood of \(x=0\),

\[y^{\prime\prime}-\tan y\,(y^{\prime})^2+4y^{\prime}+4\tan y=e^{-x}\sec y,\]
\[y(0)=\frac\pi6,\qquad y^{\prime}(0)=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad -\frac\pi2\lt y\lt \frac\pi2.\]
(a)[4]

Put \(w=\sin y\). Show that \(w^{\prime\prime}+4w^{\prime}+4w=e^{-x}\).

(b)[8]

Find the local solution for \(y\) that satisfies the initial data.

(c)[2]

Find \(y^{\prime\prime}(0)\) without differentiating the inverse sine twice.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate sin y twice, then multiply the original equation by cos y.

(b)

Translate both initial conditions to w, including the cosine factor in w′.

(c)

Use the already derived expression for w″.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The chain and product rules give

\[w^{\prime}=\cos y\,y^{\prime},\qquad w^{\prime\prime}=\cos y\,y^{\prime\prime}-\sin y\,(y^{\prime})^2.\]

Multiply the original equation by \(\cos y\), which is non-zero on the stated branch. Substitute these expressions to obtain the required linear equation.

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \((m+2)^2=0\), giving \(w_c=(A+Bx)e^{-2x}\). For a particular integral \(Ce^{-x}\), substitution gives \(C=1\). Thus

\[w=(A+Bx)e^{-2x}+e^{-x}.\]

The initial values become \(w(0)=1/2\) and \(w^{\prime}(0)=\cos(\pi/6)/\sqrt3=1/2\). Hence \(A+1=1/2\) and \(B-2A-1=1/2\), giving \(A=-1/2,B=1/2\). On the given branch,

\[y=\sin^{-1}\!\left(e^{-x}+\frac{x-1}{2}e^{-2x}\right).\]

This is the local branch through \(\pi/6\); it is used only while the inverse-sine argument stays in \((-1,1)\).

(c)

The transformed equation gives \(w^{\prime\prime}(0)=1-4(1/2)-4(1/2)=-3\). At zero the chain-rule relation gives \(-3=(\sqrt3/2)y^{\prime\prime}(0)-1/6\). Hence \(y^{\prime\prime}(0)=-17/(3\sqrt3)\).

original.title: A hyperbolic product with a global bound
original.stem_html: \[f(x)=\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
original.question_html:
\[f(x)=\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
(a)[3]

Show that \(f^{\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}x(1-2\tanh^2x)\).

(b)[5]

Find all stationary points and determine their nature.

(c)[2]

Prove directly that \(|f(x)|\le1/2\) for every real \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use both product-rule terms, then eliminate sech²x.

(b)

The first factor of f′ is strictly positive for every real x.

(c)

Complete the square in tanh²x.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The product rule gives

\[f^{\prime}=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh^2x+\operatorname{sech}x\operatorname{sech}^2x.\]

Use \(\operatorname{sech}^2x=1-\tanh^2x\) to obtain the required form.

(b)

Since \(\operatorname{sech}x\gt 0\), a stationary point requires \(\tanh^2x=1/2\). Thus \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\). At these points \(\operatorname{sech}x=1/\sqrt2\), so the values of \(f\) are \(\pm1/2\). Differentiating the factored first derivative and setting \(1-2\tanh^2x=0\) gives \(f^{\prime\prime}=-4\operatorname{sech}^3x\tanh x\). It equals \(-1\) at the positive point and \(1\) at the negative point.

(c)

Put \(v=\tanh^2x\), so \(0\le v\lt 1\). Then

\[f(x)^2=v(1-v)=\frac14-(v-\tfrac12)^2\le\frac14.\]

Taking non-negative square roots proves the bound; equality occurs at the stationary points.

original.title: A derivative determined by an implicit relation
original.stem_html:
A twice-differentiable real function satisfies

\[- 3 x - 4 y^{2} + \left(p + 2 x\right)^{3} - 4=0,\qquad y(0)=1,\]

where \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).
original.question_html:
A twice-differentiable real function satisfies

\[- 3 x - 4 y^{2} + \left(p + 2 x\right)^{3} - 4=0,\qquad y(0)=1,\]

where \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).

(a)[2]

Find \(y^{\prime}(0)\).

(b)[3]

Find \(y^{\prime\prime}(0)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the real cube root; no choice of sign is introduced.

(b)

The derivative of a bracket containing y′ also contains y″.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution gives

\[p^{3} - 8=0.\]

The real cubic root is \(p=2\).

(b)

Differentiate the relation, remembering that \(dp/dx=q=y^{\prime\prime}\):

\[3 p^{2} q + 6 p^{2} + 12 p q x + 24 p x - 8 p y + 12 q x^{2} + 24 x^{2} - 3=0.\]

At the stated point,

\[12 q + 5=0,\qquad q=- \frac{5}{12}.\]

original.title: A cubic curve with a mixed product
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{3} + 3 x y + 2 y^{3} - 9=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(-1,2)\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{3} + 3 x y + 2 y^{3} - 9=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(-1,2)\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

(b)[5]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[3 p x + 6 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} + 3 y=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[21 p + 9=0,\qquad p=- \frac{3}{7}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[12 p^{2} y + 6 p + 3 q x + 6 q y^{2} + 6 x=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[21 q - \frac{204}{49}=0,\qquad q=\frac{68}{343}.\]

original.title: An inverse tangent through an implicit relation
original.stem_html:
A curve is defined by

\[- x + \tan{\left(2 y \right)} + 1=0,\qquad x\in\mathbb R,\quad -\frac\pi4\lt y\lt \frac\pi4.\]

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).
original.question_html:
A curve is defined by

\[- x + \tan{\left(2 y \right)} + 1=0,\qquad x\in\mathbb R,\quad -\frac\pi4\lt y\lt \frac\pi4.\]

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to prove that

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=p^{2} \left(4 - 4 x\right).\]
(b)[2]

Hence find the exact second derivative at \((2,\frac{\pi}{8})\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate twice before using the original relation.

(b)

Evaluate the first derivative as well as the trigonometric factor.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[p \left(2 \tan^{2}{\left(2 y \right)} + 2\right) - 1=0.\]

Differentiate once more:

\[8 p^{2} \tan^{3}{\left(2 y \right)} + 8 p^{2} \tan{\left(2 y \right)} + 2 q \tan^{2}{\left(2 y \right)} + 2 q=0.\]

Use \(1+\tan^2 2y=1+(x-1)^2\). The first relation is \(2[1+(x-1)^2]p=1\). Its derivative gives \(4(x-1)p+2[1+(x-1)^2]q=0\). Substitute \([1+(x-1)^2]^{-1}=2p\) to obtain

\[q=p^{2} \left(4 - 4 x\right).\]

(b)

The first differentiated relation gives \(p=\frac{1}{4}\). Substituting into the identity gives

\[q=- \frac{1}{4}.\]

original.title: A zero gradient without a maximum or minimum
original.stem_html: \[f(x)=\sinh^{-1}(2x)-\tan^{-1}(2x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
original.question_html:
\[f(x)=\sinh^{-1}(2x)-\tan^{-1}(2x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
(a)[3]

Find \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and determine its sign.

(b)[4]

Find the first non-zero term in the Maclaurin expansion of \(f\).

(c)[4]

Classify the stationary point at the origin and state its tangent. Justify that the concavity changes there.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Compare a number greater than 1 with its square root.

(b)

The linear terms cancel. Compute the third derivative.

(c)

A zero first derivative does not automatically imply a turning point.
original.answer_html:
(a)

Positive for \(x\ne0\); zero only at \(x=0\).

(b)

\(f(x)=\frac43x^3+O(x^5)\).

(c)

Stationary inflection at \((0,0)\); tangent \(y=0\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=- \frac{2}{4 x^{2} + 1} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1}}.\]

For \(x\ne0\), \(1+4x^2\gt 1\) and its square root is smaller than itself. Therefore the first reciprocal is larger and \(f^{\prime}(x)\gt 0\). At zero \(f^{\prime}(0)=0\).

(b)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3+O(x^{4}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=\frac{2 \left(4 x^{2} - \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} + 1\right)}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=\frac{16 x}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}} - \frac{8 x}{\left(4 x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(3)}(x)=\frac{8 \left(8 x^{2} \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} - 24 x^{2} - \sqrt{4 x^{2} + 1} + 2\right)}{64 x^{6} + 48 x^{4} + 12 x^{2} + 1}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=8.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3}+O(x^{4}).\]

Both inverse functions are odd, so the next possible non-zero power is fifth.

(c)

The positive gradient on both sides shows that the origin is neither a maximum nor a minimum. Also

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{8x\,[2-\sqrt{1+4x^2}]}{(1+4x^2)^2}.\]

For \(|x|\lt \sqrt3/2\) the bracket is positive. Thus the second derivative changes from negative to positive at zero. The origin is a stationary point of inflection, with tangent \(y=0\).

original.title: Changing the independent variable by a cube
original.stem_html: Let \(t=x^3\) with \(x\gt 0\), and regard \(y\) as a function of \(t\).
original.question_html:
Let \(t=x^3\) with \(x\gt 0\), and regard \(y\) as a function of \(t\).

(a)[4]

Express \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) in terms of derivatives with respect to \(t\).

(b)[3]

Hence transform

\[y^{\prime\prime}-\left(\frac2x+9x^2\right)y^{\prime}+18x^4y=9x^4e^{-x^3}.\]

into a constant-coefficient equation in \(t\).

(c)[4]

Find the general solution in terms of \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The factor 3x² must also be differentiated.

(b)

Collect the y_t terms before dividing.

(c)

Solve the constant-coefficient equation before substituting back.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\frac{dt}{dx}=3x^2\),

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2\frac{dy}{dt}.\]

Differentiate this product with respect to \(x\):

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x\frac{dy}{dt}+9x^4\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}.\]

Equivalently replace \(x\) by \(t^{1/3}\).

(b)

Substitute the expressions from part (a):

\[6xy_t+9x^4y_{tt}-(2/x+9x^2)(3x^2y_t)+18x^4y=9x^4e^{-t}.\]

The terms \(6xy_t\) cancel. Divide by \(9x^4\gt 0\) to obtain

\[y_{tt}-3y_t+2y=e^{-t}.\]

(c)

The auxiliary equation \(m^2-3m+2=0\) has roots \(1,2\). For a particular integral \(ce^{-t}\), the multiplier is \(1+3+2=6\), so \(c=1/6\). Therefore

\[y=Ae^{x^3}+Be^{2x^3}+\frac16e^{-x^3},\qquad x\gt 0.\]

original.title: A cubic and a negative branch
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{3} + 4 x y + 2 y^{2} - 2=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(0,-1)\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{3} + 4 x y + 2 y^{2} - 2=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(0,-1)\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

(b)[4]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[4 p x + 4 p y + 3 x^{2} + 4 y=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[- 4 p - 4=0,\qquad p=-1.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[4 p^{2} + 8 p + 4 q x + 4 q y + 6 x=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[- 4 q - 4=0,\qquad q=-1.\]

original.title: Unequal scales on an astroid
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=3 \cos^{3}{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=5 \sin^{3}{\left(t \right)},\qquad 0\lt t\lt \frac\pi2.\]
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=3 \cos^{3}{\left(t \right)},\qquad y=5 \sin^{3}{\left(t \right)},\qquad 0\lt t\lt \frac\pi2.\]
(a)[2]

Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) in terms of \(t\).

(b)[2]

Find \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) in terms of \(t\), simplifying your answer.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

(b)

A second derivative requires a second division by dx/dt.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=- 9 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=15 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{5 \tan{\left(t \right)}}{3}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{5 \left(\tan^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1\right)}{3}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{5}{27 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos^{4}{\left(t \right)}}.\]

original.title: Two stationary points on a hyperbola
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[- 9 y^{2} + \left(x + 2 y\right)^{2} + 36=0.\]
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[- 9 y^{2} + \left(x + 2 y\right)^{2} + 36=0.\]
(a)[3]

Find a relation between \(x\) and \(y\) at a regular stationary point.

(b)[3]

Find all stationary points in the stated domain.

(c)[4]

Find the second derivative at each stationary point and determine its nature.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Set y′=0 only after obtaining the full derivative relation.

(b)

Substitute the relation from part (a) into the curve and retain every permitted root.

(c)

Differentiate before putting the first derivative equal to zero.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(2 \left(x + 2 y\right)=0\).

(b)

\((-4,2),\quad (4,-2)\).

(c)

\((-4,2)\text{, local minimum};\quad (4,-2)\text{, local maximum}\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[4 p x - 10 p y + 2 x + 4 y=0.\]

At a regular stationary point \(p=0\), so

\[2 \left(x + 2 y\right)=0.\]

(b)

On the requested branch, the stationary relation gives \(y=- \frac{x}{2}\). Substitute this in the original equation:

\[- \frac{9 \left(x - 4\right) \left(x + 4\right)}{4}=0.\]

Solving and substituting back gives the following admissible points:

\((-4,2)\): \(p=0\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(-36\), which is non-zero.

\((4,-2)\): \(p=0\) and the coefficient of \(p\) is \(36\), which is non-zero.

(c)

Differentiate the first relation again:

\[- 10 p^{2} + 8 p + 4 q x - 10 q y + 2=0.\]

At a stationary point \(p=0\). Evaluate the remaining equation separately at each point.

At \((-4,2)\),

\[2 - 36 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{1}{18}.\]

Thus this point is a local minimum.

At \((4,-2)\),

\[36 q + 2=0,\qquad q=- \frac{1}{18}.\]

Thus this point is a local maximum.

original.title: Local geometry of a tilted ellipse
original.stem_html:
The point \(P=(4,2)\) lies on

\[(x-2y)^2+9y^2=36.\]
original.question_html:
The point \(P=(4,2)\) lies on

\[(x-2y)^2+9y^2=36.\]
(a)[3]

Show that the tangent at \(P\) is horizontal.

(b)[4]

Find \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\) and classify the stationary point.

(c)[2]

State the equations of the tangent and normal at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate the squared bracket using the chain rule.

(b)

Do not discard the derivative of the bracket too early.

(c)

The normal is vertical rather than having a finite gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[- 4 p x + 26 p y + 2 x - 4 y=0.\]

At \(P\) this reduces to \(36p=0\), so \(p=0\).

(b)

A second differentiation gives

\[26 p^{2} - 8 p - 4 q x + 26 q y + 2=0.\]

At \(P\) with \(p=0\), \(2+36q=0\). Hence \(q=-1/18\lt 0\) and \(P\) is a local maximum of the branch.

(c)

A horizontal tangent through \((4,2)\) is \(y=2\). The perpendicular normal is vertical: \(x=4\).

original.title: A negative branch of a cubic relation
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[- 2 x^{2} y + y^{3} - 1=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(1,-1)\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[- 2 x^{2} y + y^{3} - 1=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(1,-1)\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

(b)[5]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[- 2 p x^{2} + 3 p y^{2} - 4 x y=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[p + 4=0,\qquad p=-4.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[6 p^{2} y - 8 p x - 2 q x^{2} + 3 q y^{2} - 4 y=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[q - 60=0,\qquad q=60.\]

original.title: An inverse hyperbolic function and its tangent
original.stem_html: \[f(x)=x\cosh^{-1}x-\sqrt{x^2-1},\qquad x\gt 1.\]
original.question_html:
\[f(x)=x\cosh^{-1}x-\sqrt{x^2-1},\qquad x\gt 1.\]
(a)[4]

Find and simplify \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\).

(b)[3]

Find the exact tangent at \(x=5/3\).

(c)[3]

Find the limits of \(f(x)\), \(f^{\prime}(x)\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\) as \(x\to1^+\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Do not expand the inverse hyperbolic function before differentiating.

(b)

Use the exact logarithmic value of acosh(5/3).

(c)

Evaluate each limit from the expression valid for x>1.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The product rule gives

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\cosh^{-1}x+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}-\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\cosh^{-1}x.\]

Hence \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2-1}\). The positive square root is valid because \(x\gt 1\).

(b)

Here \(\cosh^{-1}(5/3)=\ln3\) and \(\sqrt{x^2-1}=4/3\). Thus the point is \((5/3,\,(5/3)\ln3-4/3)\) and the gradient is \(\ln3\). Therefore

\[y=x\ln3-\frac43.\]

(c)

Both terms in f tend to zero, so its limit is 0. Since \(f^{\prime}(x)=\cosh^{-1}x\), the first derivative tends to 0. However \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{x^2-1}\) tends to \(+\infty\). The function and first derivative have finite one-sided limits, but the second derivative does not.

original.title: A parameter controlling the number of intersections
original.stem_html: \[f_k(x)=\cosh(2x)-k\sinh x,\qquad k\in\mathbb R.\]
original.question_html:
\[f_k(x)=\cosh(2x)-k\sinh x,\qquad k\in\mathbb R.\]
(a)[3]

Show that \(f_k\) has exactly one stationary point for each real \(k\).

(b)[5]

Find the stationary value and prove that it is the global minimum.

(c)[4]

Determine the number of real roots of \(f_k(x)=0\) for all real \(k\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out cosh x and use its strict positivity.

(b)

Use the double-angle identity at the stationary point.

(c)

Count intersections on the two monotonic arms, including the equality case.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(x=\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\).

(b)

Global minimum \(1-k^2/8\).

(c)

Two if \(|k|\gt 2\sqrt2\); one if \(|k|=2\sqrt2\); none if \(|k|\lt 2\sqrt2\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

The derivative is \(f_k^{\prime}(x)=\cosh x(4\sinh x-k)\). Since \(\cosh x\gt 0\) and \(\sinh x\) is strictly increasing onto the real line, the unique solution is \(x=\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\).

(b)

Before the stationary point \(4\sinh x-k\lt 0\); afterwards it is positive. Thus the function decreases and then increases. Using \(\cosh2x=1+2\sinh^2x\) gives

\[f_k\bigl(\sinh^{-1}(k/4)\bigr)=1+2\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)^2-k\left(\frac{k}{4}\right)=1-\frac{k^2}{8}.\]

Moreover \(f_k(x)\to+\infty\) at both ends of the real line because the \(e^{2|x|}\) contribution dominates the terms of order \(e^{|x|}\).

(c)

The two monotonic arms both tend to \(+\infty\). They meet at the minimum. Hence a negative minimum gives two distinct roots, a zero minimum gives one root with a horizontal tangent, and a positive minimum gives none. Compare \(1-k^2/8\) with zero.

original.title: A stationary point that disappears at the parameter boundary
original.stem_html: \[g_k(x)=\ln(\cosh x)-kx,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
original.question_html:
\[g_k(x)=\ln(\cosh x)-kx,\qquad x\in\mathbb R.\]
(a)[3]

Find the first and second derivatives and explain why any stationary point must be a minimum.

(b)[5]

Determine exactly which \(k\) give a stationary point. Describe the monotonicity when there is no stationary point.

(c)[4]

For \(k=3/5\), find the exact coordinates of the minimum and its tangent.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate ln(cosh x) as a logarithmic composition.

(b)

The endpoints of the range of tanh are not attained at finite x.

(c)

Evaluate the inverse tanh using its logarithmic expression.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(g_k^{\prime}=\tanh x-k,\quad g_k^{\prime\prime}=\operatorname{sech}^2x\).

(b)

Stationary point iff \(|k|\lt 1\). Strictly decreasing for \(k\ge1\) and increasing for \(k\le-1\).

(c)

\((\ln2,\,\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2)\); tangent \(y=\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[g_k^{\prime}(x)=\tanh x-k,\qquad g_k^{\prime\prime}(x)=\operatorname{sech}^2x\gt 0.\]

A zero first derivative therefore gives a strict local minimum; the strict increase of the first derivative makes it unique.

(b)

The range of \(\tanh x\) is \((-1,1)\), with endpoints never attained. Hence a stationary point exists exactly when \(|k|\lt 1\), and then \(x=\tanh^{-1}k\). For \(k\ge1\) the first derivative is strictly negative everywhere. For \(k\le-1\) it is strictly positive everywhere. There is no stationary point at the boundary values \(k=\pm1\).

(c)

Since \(\tanh(\ln2)=3/5\), the minimum occurs at \(x=\ln2\). Also \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\). The minimum value is \(\ln(5/4)-(3/5)\ln2\), and the tangent is horizontal at that height.

original.title: A cycloidal curve and excluded parameters
original.stem_html: \[x=6 t - 3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)},\quad y=2 - 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\quad -\pi\le t\le\pi.\]
original.question_html:
\[x=6 t - 3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)},\quad y=2 - 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\quad -\pi\le t\le\pi.\]
(a)[4]

Show that \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac23\cot t\) wherever it exists as a finite derivative. State all exceptional parameter values.

(b)[3]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) when \(t=\pi/6\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Check zeros of dx/dt before cancelling trigonometric factors.

(b)

Divide the derivative of cot t by dx/dt.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=6 - 6 \cos{\left(2 t \right)},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \cot{\left(t \right)}}{3}.\]

Here \(\frac{dx}{dt}=12\sin^2t\). It vanishes at \(t=-\pi,0,\pi\) in the stated interval. The quotient cannot be used at these cusp parameters, and \(\cot t\) has no finite limit there.

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(\cot^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1\right)}{3}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{1}{18 \sin^{4}{\left(t \right)}}.\]

At \(t=\pi/6\), this gives \(-8/9\).

original.title: Concavity on a monotonic parametric branch
original.stem_html: \[x=- t^{2} + 6 t,\quad y=2 - 2 e^{- t},\quad 0\le t\lt 3.\]
original.question_html:
\[x=- t^{2} + 6 t,\quad y=2 - 2 e^{- t},\quad 0\le t\lt 3.\]
(a)[5]

Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) in terms of \(t\).

(b)[3]

Find the point of inflection and justify your answer.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the quotient rule to the first derivative in t.

(b)

A zero of y″ must be accompanied by a change of sign.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=6 - 2 t,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2 e^{- t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{e^{- t}}{3 - t}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{\left(t - 2\right) e^{- t}}{\left(t - 3\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\left(t - 2\right) e^{- t}}{2 \left(3 - t\right)^{3}}.\]

(b)

On \(0\le t\lt 3\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=6-2t\gt 0\), so increasing \(t\) also increases \(x\). The denominator and exponential factor in the second derivative are positive; its sign changes from negative to positive at \(t=2\). The point is \((8,2-2e^{-2})\).

original.stem_html:
For \(x\gt -1\), a function satisfies

\[(x+1)^2y^{\prime\prime}+[(x+1)^2+4(x+1)]y^{\prime}+[2+2(x+1)-2(x+1)^2]y=6\sin x-2\cos x.\]
original.question_html:

\[(x+1)^2y^{\prime\prime}+[(x+1)^2+4(x+1)]y^{\prime}+[2+2(x+1)-2(x+1)^2]y=6\sin x-2\cos x.\]
(a)[4]

The curve \(C\) is defined by

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(3,0)\).

The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x^{2} + 2 x y - 3 y^{2} - 9=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(3,0)\).

original.title: A monotonic combination of coth and cosech
original.stem_html: \[f(x)=\coth x-2\operatorname{cosech}x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
\[f(x)=\coth x-2\operatorname{cosech}x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]
(a)[3]

Differentiate and prove that \(f\) is strictly increasing.

(b)[3]

Find the limits as \(x\to0^+\) and \(x\to\infty\). Hence state the range.

(c)[3]

Find the exact zero of \(f\) and justify its uniqueness.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Write both derivatives over sinh²x.

(b)

Check the sign of the small positive denominator near zero.

(c)

Reduce the equation to a cosh value and retain x>0.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}=-\operatorname{cosech}^2x+2\operatorname{cosech}x\coth x=\frac{2\cosh x-1}{\sinh^2x}.\]

For \(x\gt 0\), \(\cosh x\gt 1\) and \(\sinh^2x\gt 0\), so the derivative is strictly positive.

(b)

Write \(f=(\cosh x-2)/\sinh x\). As \(x\to0^+\), the numerator tends to \(-1\) and the denominator tends to zero from above, giving \(-\infty\). In exponential form, division by \(e^x\) gives the limit \(1\) at infinity. By continuity and strict increase, the range is \((-\infty,1)\).

(c)

The denominator is non-zero, so \(f=0\) gives \(\cosh x=2\). Therefore \(x=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\). The other solution of the unrestricted cosh equation is negative and is excluded; strict increase proves uniqueness on the given domain.

original.title: One conic, two kinds of tangent and a local expansion
original.stem_html: \[x^2+2xy+4y^2=4.\]
original.question_html:
\[x^2+2xy+4y^2=4.\]
(a)[4]

Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \((0,1)\).

(b)[3]

Find the Maclaurin expansion through \(x^2\) of the branch through \((0,1)\).

(c)[4]

Find all points with horizontal tangents and classify them as stationary points of their local branches.

(d)[3]

Find all points with vertical tangents.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the twice-differentiated relation, retaining all product terms.

(b)

The given point selects one of the two branches.

(c)

Set the numerator to zero and check that the denominator is non-zero.

(d)

Exchange the roles of x and y to justify a vertical tangent.
original.solution_html:
(a)

With \(p=y^{\prime}\) and \(q=y^{\prime\prime}\), differentiating once and twice gives

\[2x+2y+(2x+8y)p=0,\]
\[2+4p+8p^2+(2x+8y)q=0.\]

At \((0,1)\) these give \(p=-1/4\) and \(2-1+1/2+8q=0\), hence \(q=-3/16\).

(b)

The branch has \(y(0)=1\). Insert the two derivatives into the Maclaurin formula:

\[y=1-\frac14x-\frac{3}{32}x^2+O(x^3).\]

The other branch passes through \((0,-1)\) and must not be used.

(c)

For a horizontal tangent, \(p=0\) gives \(x=-y\). The curve then gives \(3y^2=4\). Thus the points are \((-2/\sqrt3,2/\sqrt3)\) and \((2/\sqrt3,-2/\sqrt3)\). At them \(q=-1/(3y)\), so the first is a local maximum and the second a local minimum.

(d)

A vertical tangent occurs when \(2x+8y=0\) but \(2x+2y\ne0\). Thus \(x=-4y\) and the curve gives \(12y^2=4\). The points are \((-4/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3)\) and \((4/\sqrt3,-1/\sqrt3)\). At both points the numerator is non-zero.

original.title: The three parameter regimes of an inverse-hyperbolic curve
original.stem_html: \[f_k(x)=\sinh^{-1}(kx)-x,\qquad k\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
\[f_k(x)=\sinh^{-1}(kx)-x,\qquad k\gt 0.\]
(a)[3]

Find the first and second derivatives.

(b)[5]

For \(k\ne1\), determine the number and nature of stationary points, giving their \(x\)-coordinates.

(c)[4]

For \(k=1\), classify the origin and find the first non-zero Maclaurin term.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the chain rule with the factor k.

(b)

The square-root equation already constrains the parameter.

(c)

Treat the boundary parameter separately rather than merging two extrema.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} x^{2} + 1}} - 1\) and \(- \frac{k^{3} x}{\left(k^{2} x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\).

(b)

None for \(0\lt k\lt 1\). For \(k\gt 1\): minimum at \(-\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\), maximum at \(\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\).

(c)

Stationary inflection; \(-x^3/6+O(x^5)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f_k^{\prime}(x)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{k^{2} x^{2} + 1}} - 1.\]
\[f_k^{\prime\prime}(x)=- \frac{k^{3} x}{\left(k^{2} x^{2} + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(b)

The stationary equation is \(\sqrt{1+k^2x^2}=k\). Both sides are non-negative and \(k\gt 0\), so squaring is valid and gives \(k^2x^2=k^2-1\). If \(0\lt k\lt 1\) this has no real solution. If \(k\gt 1\) there are two: \(x=\pm\sqrt{k^2-1}/k\). The sign of the second derivative is opposite to the sign of \(x\), so the negative point is a local minimum and the positive point a local maximum.

(c)

Now \(f^{\prime}(x)=1/\sqrt{1+x^2}-1\), which is negative for \(x\ne0\) and zero at zero. The second derivative \(-x/(1+x^2)^{3/2}\) changes from positive to negative. Thus the origin is a stationary inflection, not an extremum. At zero \(f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)=f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\) and \(f^{(3)}(0)=-1\), giving

\[f(x)=-\frac16x^3+O(x^5).\]

original.title: A positive branch of a cubic loop
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[x^{3} - 6 x y + 2 y^{3}=0.\]

Restrict attention to \(x\gt 0,\ y\gt 0\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation

\[x^{3} - 6 x y + 2 y^{3}=0.\]

Restrict attention to \(x\gt 0,\ y\gt 0\).

(a)[3]

Find a relation between \(x\) and \(y\) at a regular stationary point.

(b)[5]

Find all stationary points in the stated domain.

(c)[4]

Find the second derivative at each stationary point and determine its nature.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Set y′=0 only after obtaining the full derivative relation.

(b)

Substitute the relation from part (a) into the curve and retain every permitted root.

(c)

Differentiate before putting the first derivative equal to zero.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(q=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). Implicit differentiation gives

\[- 6 p x + 6 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} - 6 y=0.\]

At a regular stationary point \(p=0\), so

\[3 \left(x^{2} - 2 y\right)=0.\]

(b)

On the requested branch, the stationary relation gives \(y=\frac{x^{2}}{2}\). Substitute this in the original equation:

\[\frac{x^{3} \left(x - 2\right) \left(x^{2} + 2 x + 4\right)}{4}=0.\]

Discard \(x=0\) because it is excluded by the stated domain.

original.title: A square substitution and a positive solution branch
original.stem_html:
For \(x\ge0\), a positive function \(y\) satisfies

\[2yy^{\prime\prime}+2(y^{\prime})^2+6yy^{\prime}+2y^2=2x+3,\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y^{\prime}(0)=-\frac14.\]
original.question_html:
For \(x\ge0\), a positive function \(y\) satisfies

\[2yy^{\prime\prime}+2(y^{\prime})^2+6yy^{\prime}+2y^2=2x+3,\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y^{\prime}(0)=-\frac14.\]
(a)[4]

Put \(w=y^2\) and derive a linear differential equation for \(w\).

(b)[7]

Find \(y\) satisfying the initial data.

(c)[3]

Show that \(y/\sqrt{x}\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The second derivative of y² contains two terms.

(b)

Translate y′(0) into w′(0) before solving for constants.

(c)

Compare the square of y with x before taking the limit.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[w^{\prime}=2yy^{\prime},\qquad w^{\prime\prime}=2(y^{\prime})^2+2yy^{\prime\prime}.\]

Substitution gives

\[w^{\prime\prime}+3w^{\prime}+2w=2x+3.\]

(b)

The auxiliary roots are \(-1,-2\). A trial \(cx+d\) gives \(c=1,d=0\). Hence \(w=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+x\). The initial data become \(w(0)=4\) and \(w^{\prime}(0)=2(2)(-1/4)=-1\). Thus \(A+B=4\) and \(-A-2B+1=-1\), giving \(A=6,B=-2\). The positive branch is

\[y=\sqrt{x+6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}}.\]

For \(x\ge0\), \(6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}=2e^{-x}(3-e^{-x})\gt 0\), so this branch remains real and positive.

(c)

For \(x\gt 0\),

\[\frac{y}{\sqrt x}=\sqrt{1+\frac{6e^{-x}-2e^{-2x}}x}.\]

The exponential terms divided by \(x\) tend to zero. Continuity of the positive square root gives the limit 1.

original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[2 x^{2} y + 3 x y^{2} + 8=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(-1,2)\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[2 x^{2} y + 3 x y^{2} + 8=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(-1,2)\).

(a)[3]

(b)[5]

(a)

(b)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[2 p x^{2} + 6 p x y + 4 x y + 3 y^{2}=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[\frac{336}{25} - 10 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{168}{125}.\]

original.title: Recovering an inverse-sine function from derivatives
original.stem_html:
A function has the form \(f(x)=a\sin^{-1}(x/b)+c\), where \(a\gt 0\), \(b\gt 0\) and \(c\) is real. It satisfies

\[f(0)=1,\qquad f^{\prime}(0)=2,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=\frac12.\]
original.question_html:
A function has the form \(f(x)=a\sin^{-1}(x/b)+c\), where \(a\gt 0\), \(b\gt 0\) and \(c\) is real. It satisfies

\[f(0)=1,\qquad f^{\prime}(0)=2,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=\frac12.\]
(a)[5]

Find \(a,b,c\).

(b)[3]

State the real domain of \(f\) and find its second derivative on the interior.

(c)[3]

Find the tangent at \(x=1\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the first and third derivatives at zero to remove the scale factor.

(b)

The endpoints belong to the function domain but not to the finite-derivative formula.

(c)

Evaluate both the function and its gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

At zero \(c=1\). Differentiation gives \(f^{\prime}=a/\sqrt{b^2-x^2}\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}=ax(b^2-x^2)^{-3/2}\). Hence \(f^{\prime}(0)=a/b=2\) and \(f^{(3)}(0)=a/b^3=1/2\). Dividing gives \(b^2=4\). The positive root is \(b=2\), and \(a=4\).

(b)

The inverse sine is real when \(|x/2|\le1\), so the domain is \([-2,2]\). The finite differentiable interior is \((-2,2)\), where

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{4 x}{\left(4 - x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(c)

The point is \((1,1+2\pi/3)\) and its gradient is \(4/\sqrt3\). Thus

\[y=1+\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac4{\sqrt3}(x-1).\]

original.title: A logarithmic curve just touching the axis
original.stem_html: \[g_a(x)=\ln(1+ae^x)-\frac23x,\qquad a\gt 0,\quad x\in\mathbb R.\]
original.question_html:
\[g_a(x)=\ln(1+ae^x)-\frac23x,\qquad a\gt 0,\quad x\in\mathbb R.\]
(a)[3]

Find the first two derivatives and show that the second is positive.

(b)[5]

Find the exact global minimum in terms of \(a\).

(c)[3]

Find the value of \(a\) for which the \(x\)-axis is tangent to the curve.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate the logarithm and then its rational derivative.

(b)

Solve first for ae^x, then recover x.

(c)

A horizontal contact with the axis occurs at the minimum.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[g_a^{\prime}(x)=\frac{ae^x}{1+ae^x}-\frac23,\qquad g_a^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{ae^x}{(1+ae^x)^2}\gt 0.\]

The sign follows from \(a\gt 0\) and \(e^x\gt 0\).

(b)

Set the first derivative to zero: \(3ae^x=2(1+ae^x)\), so \(ae^x=2\) and \(x=\ln(2/a)\). The strictly increasing gradient is negative before and positive after this point. Therefore the minimum is global and equals

\[\ln3-\frac23\ln(2/a).\]

(c)

The minimum must be zero. Hence \(\ln(2/a)=\frac32\ln3\) and \(2/a=3\sqrt3\). Therefore \(a=2/(3\sqrt3)\).

(a)[4]

Put \(u=\ln(x+2)\) and transform the differential equation into an equation in \(u\).

(b)[5]

Find the general solution in terms of \(x\).

(c)[3]

Use the initial data to find the particular solution.

(d)[2]

Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y/x^3\).

(a)

The second derivative includes a derivative of 1/(x+2).

(b)

(c)

(d)

Identify the leading power after expanding or taking ratios.

(a)

Because \(du/dx=1/(x+2)\),

\[y_x=\frac{y_u}{x+2},\qquad y_{xx}=\frac{y_{uu}-y_u}{(x+2)^2}.\]

Substitution gives

\[y_{uu}-2y_u-3y=5e^{2u}.\]

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \((m-3)(m+1)=0\). For \(ce^{2u}\), substitution gives \((4-4-3)c=5\), so \(c=-5/3\). Thus

\[y=A(x+2)^3+\frac{B}{x+2}-\frac53(x+2)^2.\]

(c)

At \(x=-1\), \(x+2=1\). The equations are \(A+B=5/3\) and \(3A-B=13/3\). Solving gives \(A=3/2,B=1/6\).

(d)

Divide each term by \(x^3\). The cubic term tends to \(3/2\) and the other terms tend to zero.

original.title: Second derivative on a parametric ellipse
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=4 \sin{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad y=2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad 0\lt t\lt \frac\pi3.\]
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=4 \sin{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad y=2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad 0\lt t\lt \frac\pi3.\]
(a)[3]

Find the exact gradient at \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

(b)[4]

Find the exact second derivative at the same point.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

(b)

A second derivative requires a second division by dx/dt.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=12 \cos{\left(3 t \right)},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=- 6 \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=- \frac{\tan{\left(3 t \right)}}{2}.\]

At \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\), the gradient is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{3 \left(\tan^{2}{\left(3 t \right)} + 1\right)}{2}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{1}{8 \cos^{3}{\left(3 t \right)}}.\]

At \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\), the second derivative is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\).

original.title: The absolute value hidden by a principal inverse
original.stem_html:
\[f(x)=\cosh^{-1}(1+x^2),\qquad x\in\mathbb R,\]

where \(\cosh^{-1}\) denotes the non-negative principal value.
original.question_html:
\[f(x)=\cosh^{-1}(1+x^2),\qquad x\in\mathbb R,\]

where \(\cosh^{-1}\) denotes the non-negative principal value.

(a)[4]

Show that \(f(x)=2\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\).

(b)[4]

Find the first and second derivatives separately for \(x\gt 0\) and \(x\lt 0\).

(c)[3]

Find the two one-sided derivatives at zero and decide whether \(f\) is differentiable there.

(d)[2]

Explain why the usual derivative-based Maclaurin expansion cannot be applied to \(f\) at zero.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosh cannot return a negative value.

(b)

Handle the derivative of |x| separately on each side.

(c)

Use a difference quotient at zero; the off-zero formula cannot simply be substituted.

(d)

The obstruction already occurs at the first derivative.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(2\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\).

(b)

First derivative has the two signs above; \(f^{\prime\prime}=-2|x|/(x^2+2)^{3/2}\).

(c)

Left \(-\sqrt2\), right \(\sqrt2\); not differentiable.

(d)

No two-sided Maclaurin representation; the leading term is \(\sqrt2|x|\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\sinh^{-1}(|x|/\sqrt2)\ge0\). Then \(\cosh(2u)=1+2\sinh^2u=1+x^2\). Since \(2u\ge0\), it is the principal inverse-cosh value. Thus \(f=2u\).

(b)

For \(x\gt 0\), differentiate \(2\sinh^{-1}(x/\sqrt2)\). For \(x\lt 0\), differentiate \(2\sinh^{-1}(-x/\sqrt2)\). The results are

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\begin{cases}2/\sqrt{x^2+2},&x\gt 0,\\-2/\sqrt{x^2+2},&x\lt 0,\end{cases}\]
\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-\frac{2|x|}{(x^2+2)^{3/2}},\qquad x\ne0.\]

(c)

Since \(f(0)=0\) and \(\sinh^{-1}u/u\to1\) as \(u\to0\) (from the derivative of \(\sinh^{-1}u\) at zero), the right difference quotient tends to \(\sqrt2\) and the left to \(-\sqrt2\). They differ, so there is no derivative at zero.

(d)

The Maclaurin formula requires the derivatives at zero. Here even the first derivative at zero does not exist, so the usual derivative-based expansion is unavailable. The leading behaviour is \(\sqrt2|x|\), not a single linear term valid on both sides.

original.title: An implicit product of two factors
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[\left(x + 2 y\right) \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right) - 2=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(0,1)\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[\left(x + 2 y\right) \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right) - 2=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(0,1)\).

(a)[3]

Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

(b)[4]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[2 p x^{2} + 2 p x y + 6 p y^{2} + 3 x^{2} + 4 x y + y^{2}=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[6 p + 1=0,\qquad p=- \frac{1}{6}.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[2 p^{2} x + 12 p^{2} y + 8 p x + 4 p y + 2 q x^{2} + 2 q x y + 6 q y^{2} + 6 x + 4 y=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[6 q + \frac{11}{3}=0,\qquad q=- \frac{11}{18}.\]

original.title: A stationary point specified by a unique transcendental root
original.stem_html: \[f_k(x)=x\operatorname{sech}(kx),\qquad k\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
\[f_k(x)=x\operatorname{sech}(kx),\qquad k\gt 0.\]
(a)[3]

Find \(f_k^{\prime}(x)\) and show that a positive stationary point satisfies \(u\tanh u=1\), where \(u=kx\).

(b)[4]

Prove that this equation has exactly one positive root \(u=\alpha\) and verify \(1.19\lt \alpha\lt 1.20\).

(c)[4]

Find both stationary points in terms of \(k\) and \(\alpha\), and classify them.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out sech(kx).

(b)

Separate existence, uniqueness and the numerical bracket.

(c)

Use the symmetry of u tanh u, not of f itself.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f_k^{\prime}(x)=\left(- k x \tanh{\left(k x \right)} + 1\right) \operatorname{sech}{\left(k x \right)}.\]

The sech factor is positive. Thus the stationary equation is \(kx\tanh(kx)=1\).

(b)

Let \(H(u)=u\tanh u\) for \(u\gt 0\). Then \(H^{\prime}(u)=\tanh u+u\operatorname{sech}^2u\gt 0\). Also \(H(0)=0\) and \(H(u)\to\infty\). Continuity and strict increase give exactly one crossing of 1. Numerically, \(H(1.19)-1\approx-0.011611146\) and \(H(1.20)-1\approx0.00038552841\).

(c)

The function \(u\tanh u\) is even, so the two stationary parameters are \(\pm\alpha\). The points are \((\alpha/k,\,\alpha\operatorname{sech}\alpha/k)\) and its negative. The derivative is positive between them and negative outside. Thus the negative point is a local minimum and the positive point a local maximum.

original.title: A resonant term after an exponential substitution
original.stem_html:
For \(x\gt 0\), the function \(y\) satisfies

\[x^2y^{\prime\prime}+2xy^{\prime}-6y=10x^2.\]
original.question_html:
For \(x\gt 0\), the function \(y\) satisfies

\[x^2y^{\prime\prime}+2xy^{\prime}-6y=10x^2.\]
(a)[3]

With \(x=e^u\), show that \(xy_x=y_u\) and \(x^2y_{xx}=y_{uu}-y_u\).

(b)[3]

Transform the differential equation and find its complementary function.

(c)[5]

A suitable particular integral has the form \(cu e^{2u}\). Determine \(c\) and find the general solution in terms of \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate y_u/x using both the product and chain rules.

(b)

The forcing exponential repeats one of the complementary-function exponents.

(c)

Differentiate the supplied trial form instead of guessing an unsupported form.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(du/dx=1/x\), \(y_x=y_u/x\). Differentiating once more gives \(y_{xx}=(y_{uu}-y_u)/x^2\).

(b)

Substitution yields \(y_{uu}+y_u-6y=10e^{2u}\). The auxiliary equation is \((m-2)(m+3)=0\), so \(y_c=Ae^{2u}+Be^{-3u}\).

\[(y_p)_u=c(1+2u)e^{2u},\qquad (y_p)_{uu}=c(4+4u)e^{2u}.\]

Thus \((y_p)_{uu}+(y_p)_u-6y_p=5ce^{2u}\). Equating this with \(10e^{2u}\) gives \(c=2\). Therefore

\[y=Ax^2+Bx^{-3}+2x^2\ln x,\qquad x\gt 0.\]

original.title: Recovering a point from its second derivative
original.stem_html:
The curve has parametric equations

\[x=\tanh^2t+2\ln(\operatorname{sech}t),\qquad y=3+3\tanh^4t,\qquad t\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
The curve has parametric equations

\[x=\tanh^2t+2\ln(\operatorname{sech}t),\qquad y=3+3\tanh^4t,\qquad t\gt 0.\]
(a)[3]

Starting with exponential definitions, prove \(\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=1\).

(b)[4]

Show that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-6\operatorname{sech}^2t\).

(c)[7]

Find the exact coordinates of the point where \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{32}{3}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Write both functions over the denominator (e^t+e^(−t))².

(b)

Simplify x_t using the identity before dividing.

(c)

Use v=tanh²t, and select the positive square root from t>0.
original.answer_html:
(a)

The identity is established by expanding the exponential numerator.

(b)

\(- 6 \operatorname{sech}^{2}{\left(t \right)}\).

(c)

\((9/25+\ln(16/25),\ 2118/625)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

From the exponential definitions,

\[\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=\frac{(e^t-e^{-t})^2+4}{(e^t+e^{-t})^2}=\frac{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}=1.\]

(b)

Using the identity from part (a),

\[x_t=2\tanh t\operatorname{sech}^2t-2\tanh t=-2\tanh^3t,\]
\[y_t=12\tanh^3t\operatorname{sech}^2t.\]

Because \(t\gt 0\), \(\tanh t\ne0\). Dividing yields \(y_x=-6\operatorname{sech}^2t\).

(c)

Differentiate the result in part (b) and divide by \(x_t\):

\[y_{xx}=\frac{12\operatorname{sech}^2t\tanh t}{-2\tanh^3t}=-\frac{6\operatorname{sech}^2t}{\tanh^2t}.\]

Let \(v=\tanh^2t\). The prescribed value gives \(6(1-v)/v=32/3\), so \(v=9/25\). Since \(t\gt 0\), \(\tanh t=3/5\) and \(\operatorname{sech}t=4/5\). Substitution in the original parametrisation gives

\[\boxed{\left(\frac9{25}+\ln\frac{16}{25},\ \frac{2118}{625}\right)}.\]

There is only one such positive parameter because tanh is strictly increasing.

original.title: An exponential parametric curve
original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=t + e^{- t},\qquad y=t - e^{- t},\qquad t\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[x=t + e^{- t},\qquad y=t - e^{- t},\qquad t\gt 0.\]
(a)[3]

Find the exact gradient at \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\).

(b)[4]

Find the exact second derivative at the same point.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

(b)

A second derivative requires a second division by dx/dt.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1 - e^{- t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=1 + e^{- t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1 + e^{- t}}{1 - e^{- t}}.\]

At \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\), the gradient is \(2\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 e^{t}}{\left(e^{t} - 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{2 e^{- t}}{\left(1 - e^{- t}\right)^{3}}.\]

At \(t=\ln{\left(3 \right)}\), the second derivative is \(- \frac{9}{4}\).

original.title: A vertical tangent and two concavity regions
original.stem_html: \[x=\frac{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 3 \sqrt{t},\quad y=2 t - 1,\quad 0\lt t\le5.\]
original.question_html:
\[x=\frac{t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 3 \sqrt{t},\quad y=2 t - 1,\quad 0\lt t\le5.\]
(a)[3]

Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and locate the vertical tangent.

(b)[4]

Find \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) wherever it is defined.

(c)[3]

Find the set of parameter values for which \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\gt 0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

A zero of dx/dt need not be a stationary point of y as a function of x.

(b)

Use the parametric second-derivative formula away from the vertical tangent.

(c)

Keep the sign of the cubed denominator.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2} - \frac{3}{2 \sqrt{t}},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4 \sqrt{t}}{t - 3}.\]

At \(t=3\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=0\) but \(\frac{dy}{dt}\ne0\). The tangent is vertical at \((- 2 \sqrt{3},5)\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(t + 3\right)}{\sqrt{t} \left(t - 3\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{- 4 t - 12}{\left(t - 3\right)^{3}}.\]

(c)

Every factor in the numerator has the displayed fixed sign on the domain. The cubed denominator changes sign at \(t=3\). Hence the second derivative is positive for \(0\lt t\lt 3\). It is undefined at the vertical tangent; that point cannot be classified as an ordinary stationary point by setting \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\).

(a)[3]

Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and locate the vertical tangent.

(b)[4]

Find \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) wherever it is defined.

(c)[2]

Find the set of parameter values for which \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\gt 0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

(b)

original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3 t}{2 t^{2} - 2}\); vertical tangent at \((1,4)\).

(b)

(a)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=2 t - \frac{2}{t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=3.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3 t}{2 t^{2} - 2}.\]

At \(t=1\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=0\) but \(\frac{dy}{dt}\ne0\). The tangent is vertical at \((1,4)\).

(b)

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{3 \left(t^{2} + 1\right)}{2 \left(t - 1\right)^{2} \left(t + 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{3 t \left(t^{2} + 1\right)}{4 \left(t^{2} - 1\right)^{3}}.\]

Every factor in the numerator has the displayed fixed sign on the domain. The cubed denominator changes sign at \(t=1\). Hence the second derivative is positive for \(0\lt t\lt 1\). It is undefined at the vertical tangent; that point cannot be classified as an ordinary stationary point by setting \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\).

original.stem_html:

At \(t=1\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\).
original.question_html:
\[x=t+\frac13t^3,\qquad y=at^2+b\ln t,\qquad t\gt 0.\]

At \(t=1\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-1\).

(a)[5]

Find \(a\) and \(b\).

(b)[5]

For these values, find the second derivative in terms of \(t\) and show that the curve has no point of inflection.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the parametric second-derivative formula before substituting t=1.

(b)

Prove a strict sign, not merely the absence of a guessed root.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=2,\ b=2\).

(b)

\(- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{3}}\); no inflection for \(t\gt 0\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 a t^{2} + b}{t^{3} + t}.\]

At \(t=1\) the gradient is \(a+b/2\). Using \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=(y_{tt}x_t-y_tx_{tt})/(x_t)^3\) gives \(-b/2\) at \(t=1\). Thus \(b=2\) and \(a=2\).

(b)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=t^{2} + 1,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=4 t + \frac{2}{t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \left(2 t^{2} + 1\right)}{t \left(t^{2} + 1\right)}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=- \frac{2 \left(2 t^{4} + t^{2} + 1\right)}{t^{2} \left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{3}}.\]

Equivalently, the second derivative is \(-\dfrac{2(2t^4+t^2+1)}{t^2(1+t^2)^3}\). Every factor in its denominator is positive and the numerator is strictly negative for \(t\gt 0\). Since \(\frac{dx}{dt}=1+t^2\gt 0\), the curve is a single regular branch and has no inflection.

original.title: From a hyperbolic parameter to a local expansion
original.stem_html:
A curve is defined for real \(t\) by

\[x=\tanh t,\qquad y=\ln(\cosh t).\]
original.question_html:
A curve is defined for real \(t\) by

\[x=\tanh t,\qquad y=\ln(\cosh t).\]
(a)[3]

Eliminate \(t\) and state the exact range of \(x\).

(b)[4]

Using the parametric equations, find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), expressing both in terms of \(x\).

(c)[3]

Find the Maclaurin expansion through the term in \(x^4\).

(d)[2]

Show that the curve has a unique global minimum, and give its coordinates.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use cosh²t=1/(1−tanh²t) and its positive square root.

(b)

Do not confuse d/dt with d/dx in the second step.

(c)

Substitute x² into the standard logarithm series.

(d)

Use the sign of the first derivative over the entire domain.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(y=-\tfrac12\ln(1-x^2),\quad -1\lt x\lt 1\).

(b)

\(y_x=x/(1-x^2),\quad y_{xx}=(1+x^2)/(1-x^2)^2\).

(c)

\(\frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{x^{2}}{2}\)\(+O(x^6)\).

(d)

\((0,0)\) is the unique global minimum.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The identity \(1-\tanh^2t=\operatorname{sech}^2t\) gives \(\cosh^2t=1/(1-x^2)\). Since \(\cosh t\gt 0\),

\[y=-\frac12\ln(1-x^2),\qquad -1\lt x\lt 1.\]

The endpoints are not reached at finite real t.

(b)

\[x_t=\operatorname{sech}^2t,\qquad y_t=\tanh t,\qquad y_x=\frac{\tanh t}{\operatorname{sech}^2t}=\frac{x}{1-x^2}.\]

A second parametric differentiation yields

\[y_{xx}=\frac{\cosh2t}{\operatorname{sech}^2t}=\frac{1+x^2}{(1-x^2)^2}.\]

Here \(\cosh2t=(1+x^2)/(1-x^2)\).

(c)

Use \(\ln(1-z)=-z-z^2/2+O(z^3)\) with \(z=x^2\). Hence

\[y=\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{4}+O(x^6).\]

(d)

The denominator of \(y_x=x/(1-x^2)\) is positive. Thus y decreases for x<0 and increases for x>0. Its only minimum is \((0,0)\).

original.title: A stationary point with a vanishing second derivative
original.stem_html:
A curve is defined by

\[x=t+\ln t,\qquad y=t^2-at+b\ln t,\qquad t\gt 0,\]

where \(a,b\) are real constants. At \(t=1\), both \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) are zero.
original.question_html:
A curve is defined by

\[x=t+\ln t,\qquad y=t^2-at+b\ln t,\qquad t\gt 0,\]

where \(a,b\) are real constants. At \(t=1\), both \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) are zero.

(a)[4]

Find \(a\) and \(b\).

(b)[4]

For these constants, find and factorise both derivatives in terms of \(t\).

(c)[3]

Determine the nature of the point with \(t=1\) and give its tangent.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the first condition to simplify the second-derivative formula at t=1.

(b)

Factor the first derivative before differentiating it.

(c)

Check signs on both sides; y″=0 alone does not classify a point.
original.solution_html:
(a)

At \(t=1\), \(x_t=2\). The condition \(y_x=0\) is \(y_t=2-a+b=0\). At a point where \(y_t=0\), the parametric formula gives \(y_{xx}=y_{tt}/x_t^2\). Since \(y_{tt}(1)=2-b\), the second condition gives \(b=2\), and then \(a=4\).

(b)

\[\frac{dx}{dt}=1 + \frac{1}{t},\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=2 t - 4 + \frac{2}{t}.\]

Where \(\frac{dx}{dt}\ne0\), divide the two derivatives:

\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right)^{2}}{t + 1}.\]

Differentiate the gradient with respect to \(t\) and then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}.\]
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right) \left(t + 3\right)}{\left(t + 1\right)^{2}}.\]
\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{2 t \left(t - 1\right) \left(t + 3\right)}{\left(t + 1\right)^{3}}.\]

(c)

The first derivative is non-negative for all t>0 and positive except at t=1, so there is no local maximum or minimum. The second derivative is negative for 0<t<1 and positive for t>1. Since x_t>0, this is also a change of concavity as x increases. Therefore \((1,-3)\) is a stationary point of inflection. Its tangent is \(y=-3\).

original.title: An inverse sine of a hyperbolic function
original.stem_html: Define \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}(\tanh2x)\) for real \(x\), using the principal inverse sine.
original.question_html:
Define \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}(\tanh2x)\) for real \(x\), using the principal inverse sine.

(a)[3]

Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(1-\tanh^2u=\operatorname{sech}^2u\).

(b)[3]

Show that \(f^{\prime}(x)=2\operatorname{sech}2x\), explaining the sign of the square root used.

(c)[2]

Find the exact value of \(f^{\prime\prime}(\tfrac12\ln2)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Subtract the squared exponential numerators.

(b)

The square root of a square is an absolute value until its sign has been justified.

(c)

Differentiate the simplified expression, retaining the factor 2.
original.solution_html:
(a)

From the exponential definitions,

\[\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=\frac{(e^t-e^{-t})^2+4}{(e^t+e^{-t})^2}=\frac{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}=1.\]

Rearrange the identity, with the argument renamed u.

(b)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{sech}^22x}{\sqrt{1-\tanh^22x}}.\]

By part (a), the denominator is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{sech}^22x}=|\operatorname{sech}2x|\). For real x, cosh is positive, hence sech is positive. Therefore the denominator is sech2x, giving the required result.

(c)

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-4\operatorname{sech}2x\tanh2x.\]

At \(2x=\ln2\), sech is 4/5 and tanh is 3/5. Hence \(f^{\prime\prime}=-48/25\).

original.stem_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[4 y^{2} - 5 \sinh^{-1}{\left(x y \right)} - 1 + 5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})\).
original.question_html:
The curve \(C\) is defined by

\[4 y^{2} - 5 \sinh^{-1}{\left(x y \right)} - 1 + 5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}=0.\]

Consider its smooth local branch through \(P=(\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})\).

(a)[4]

Use implicit differentiation to find the exact value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(P\).

(b)[5]

Find the exact value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(P\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate products before substituting the coordinates.

(b)

Differentiate the relation from part (a), not the numerical gradient.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate the complete equation with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\):

\[8yp-\frac{5(y+xp)}{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}}=0.\]

At \(P\) this becomes

\[- 2 p - 2=0,\qquad p=-1.\]

(b)

Differentiate the first relation before substituting the point. With \(q=\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), the product and chain rules give

\[8p^2+8yq-\frac{5(2p+xq)}{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}}+\frac{5xy(y+xp)^2}{(1+x^2y^2)^{3/2}}=0.\]

Now substitute the point and the value of \(p\):

\[\frac{448}{25} - 2 q=0,\qquad q=\frac{224}{25}.\]

original.title: A Maclaurin approximation to a hyperbolic arc
original.stem_html:
A curve has parametric equations

\[x=2\cosh t,\qquad y=2\sinh t,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac14.\]

You may use \(s=\int\sqrt{x_t^2+y_t^2}\,dt\) for arc length.
original.question_html:
A curve has parametric equations

\[x=2\cosh t,\qquad y=2\sinh t,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac14.\]

You may use \(s=\int\sqrt{x_t^2+y_t^2}\,dt\) for arc length.

(a)[3]

Show that its length is \(s=2\int_0^{1/4}\sqrt{\cosh2t}\,dt\).

(b)[4]

Find the Maclaurin expansion of \(\sqrt{\cosh2t}\) through the term in \(t^4\).

(c)[2]

Hence obtain an approximation to the arc length as a rational fraction.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use cosh2t=cosh²t+sinh²t.

(b)

The t⁴ coefficient receives contributions from both z/2 and −z²/8.

(c)

Integrate the truncated polynomial, keeping the factor 2.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The derivatives are \(x_t=2\sinh t\) and \(y_t=2\cosh t\). Thus \(x_t^2+y_t^2=4(\sinh^2t+\cosh^2t)=4\cosh2t\). The speed is the positive square root, giving the stated integral.

(b)

\[\cosh2t=1+2t^2+\frac23t^4+O(t^6).\]

Use \((1+z)^{1/2}=1+z/2-z^2/8+O(z^3)\). The squared quadratic contribution must be retained:

\[\sqrt{\cosh2t}=1+t^2+\left(\frac13-\frac12\right)t^4+O(t^6)=1+t^2-\frac16t^4+O(t^6).\]

(c)

\[s\approx2\left[t+\frac{t^3}{3}-\frac{t^5}{30}\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac{2613}{5120}.\]

This is a truncated-series approximation, not an exact arc length or a proved error bound.

original.title: A parameter at the threshold of a stationary point
original.stem_html: For \(a\gt 0\), define \(f_a(x)=e^{-ax}\cosh2x\) on the whole real line.
original.question_html:
For \(a\gt 0\), define \(f_a(x)=e^{-ax}\cosh2x\) on the whole real line.

(a)[3]

Find \(f_a^{\prime}(x)\) and show that its sign is the sign of \(2\tanh2x-a\).

(b)[5]

Classify the stationary points for all \(a\gt 0\), including the case \(a=2\).

(c)[4]

When \(a=6/5\), find the exact coordinates of the minimum. Also find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f_2(x)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out a positive factor before studying signs.

(b)

The range of tanh is open: −1<tanh<1.

(c)

Use exponential forms to evaluate the exact hyperbolic values and the threshold limit.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\left(- a \cosh{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 \sinh{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{- a x}\). The sign is that of \(2\tanh2x-a\).

(b)

One global minimum for \(0\lt a\lt 2\); none for \(a\ge2\).

(c)

\((\tfrac12\ln2,\tfrac54\,2^{-3/5})\); limit \(1/2\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f_a^{\prime}(x)=\left(- a \cosh{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 \sinh{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{- a x}.\]

Factor as \(e^{-ax}\cosh2x(2\tanh2x-a)\). Both exponential and cosh factors are positive for every real x.

(b)

Because tanh2x is strictly increasing from −1 to 1, the equation \(\tanh2x=a/2\) has exactly one real root if \(0\lt a\lt 2\), namely \(x=\tfrac12\tanh^{-1}(a/2)\). The derivative changes from negative to positive, so it is a unique global minimum. If a≥2, the derivative is strictly negative at every finite x, so no stationary point exists. At a=2, the value 1 is approached by tanh but never attained; therefore the equality case must not be included among the stationary cases.

(c)

The stationary equation is \(\tanh2x=3/5\), giving \(2x=\ln2\). At this point \(\cosh2x=5/4\) and \(e^{-6x/5}=2^{-3/5}\). Thus the minimum is

\[\left(\frac12\ln2,\ \frac54\,2^{-3/5}\right).\]

For the threshold a=2, \(f_2(x)=\tfrac12(1+e^{-4x})\), so its limit is 1/2. This limiting value is not reached at a finite point.

original.title: A hyperbolic substitution in a nonlinear equation
original.stem_html:
A smooth real function \(u(x)\) satisfies

\[\cosh u\,u^{\prime\prime}+\sinh u\,(u^{\prime})^2+3\cosh u\,u^{\prime}+2\sinh u=6e^x,\]
\[u(0)=\ln(1+\sqrt2),\qquad u^{\prime}(0)=0.\]
original.question_html:
A smooth real function \(u(x)\) satisfies

\[\cosh u\,u^{\prime\prime}+\sinh u\,(u^{\prime})^2+3\cosh u\,u^{\prime}+2\sinh u=6e^x,\]
\[u(0)=\ln(1+\sqrt2),\qquad u^{\prime}(0)=0.\]
(a)[4]

Put \(w=\sinh u\) and derive the corresponding linear equation.

(b)[8]

Find \(u\) in terms of \(x\).

(c)[2]

Find \(u^{\prime\prime}(0)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate sinh u twice, retaining the squared first derivative.

(b)

Transform both initial conditions and use the real inverse sinh.

(c)

Use the transformed differential equation to evaluate w″ first.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[w^{\prime}=\cosh u\,u^{\prime},\qquad w^{\prime\prime}=\sinh u\,(u^{\prime})^2+\cosh u\,u^{\prime\prime}.\]

The equation becomes \(w^{\prime\prime}+3w^{\prime}+2w=6e^x\).

(b)

The auxiliary roots are \(-1,-2\). An exponential trial gives \(w_p=e^x\) because \(1+3+2=6\). Thus \(w=Ae^{-x}+Be^{-2x}+e^x\). The initial data are \(w(0)=1\) and \(w^{\prime}(0)=0\). Therefore \(A+B=0\) and \(-A-2B+1=0\), giving \(A=-1,B=1\). Hence

\[u=\sinh^{-1}(e^x-e^{-x}+e^{-2x}).\]

The real inverse sinh is single-valued on the whole real line, so no additional sign choice is needed.

(c)

The transformed equation gives \(w^{\prime\prime}(0)=6-2=4\). Since \(u^{\prime}(0)=0\) and \(cosh(u(0))=\sqrt2\), the chain-rule relation gives \(4=\sqrt2\,u^{\prime\prime}(0)\). Thus \(u^{\prime\prime}(0)=2\sqrt2\).

original.title: An exponential of a rational expression
original.stem_html:
Let

\[f(x)=e^{\frac{2}{3 - x}}.\]
original.question_html:
Let

\[f(x)=e^{\frac{2}{3 - x}}.\]
(a)[5]

By calculating derivatives at zero, find the Maclaurin expansion through the term in \(x^{2}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the value of f(0), including any logarithmic or exponential constant.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+O(x^{3}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=\frac{2 e^{- \frac{2}{x - 3}}}{\left(x - 3\right)^{2}}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=\frac{4 \left(4 - x\right) e^{- \frac{2}{x - 3}}}{\left(x - 3\right)^{4}}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=e^{\frac{2}{3}},\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=\frac{2 e^{\frac{2}{3}}}{9},\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=\frac{16 e^{\frac{2}{3}}}{81}.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=\frac{8 x^{2} e^{\frac{2}{3}}}{81} + \frac{2 x e^{\frac{2}{3}}}{9} + e^{\frac{2}{3}}+O(x^{3}).\]

original.title: Inverse sine and a small definite integral
original.question_html:
Let \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}(2x)\) for \(|x|\lt 1/2\).

(a)[4]

Find the Maclaurin expansion of \(f(x)\) through the term in \(x^3\).

(b)[2]

Use part (a) to approximate

\[\int_0^{1/10}\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4u^2}}\,du,\]

giving a rational fraction.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Start with f′(x)=2(1−4x²)^(−1/2).

(b)

Use the upper limit in the antiderivative expansion.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3+O(x^{4}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - 4 x^{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=\frac{8 x}{\left(1 - 4 x^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]
\[f^{(3)}(x)=\frac{8 \left(8 x^{2} + 1\right)}{\left(1 - 4 x^{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=2,\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=8.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3} + 2 x+O(x^{4}).\]

(b)

The integral equals \(\sin^{-1}(1/5)\). Evaluate the truncated series at \(x=1/10\):

\[\frac15+\frac{4}{3}\left(\frac1{10}\right)^3=\frac{151}{750}.\]

This is an approximation, not an exact evaluation of the integral.

original.stem_html:

\[(2+x)y+(1+2x+y)^3=1.\]
original.question_html:
The smooth branch through \((0,0)\) is given by

\[(2+x)y+(1+2x+y)^3=1.\]
(a)[3]

(b)[5]

(c)[2]

original.stem_html: \[f(x)=-2\ln\!\left(\cos\frac{x}{2}\right),\qquad -\pi\lt x\lt \pi.\]
original.question_html:

Find \(f^{\prime}\) and \(f^{\prime\prime}\).

(b)[3]

(c)[2]

original.hint_html:
(a)

Retain the chain-rule factors.

(b)

(c)

original.solution_html:
(a)

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\tan(x/2),\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\tfrac12\sec^2(x/2).\]

The factor \(1/2\) comes from the inner argument in each differentiation.

(b)

The function is even. At zero, \(f(0)=0,\ f^{\prime\prime}(0)=1/2,\ f^{(4)}(0)=1/4\) and its odd derivatives vanish. Therefore

\[f(x)=\frac14x^2+\frac1{96}x^4+O(x^6).\]

(c)

The coefficient of \(x^4\) is \(f^{(4)}(0)/4!\), not \(f^{(4)}(0)\). Thus \(f^{(4)}(0)=24/96=1/4\).

original.title: A reciprocal inside an inverse hyperbolic function
original.stem_html: \[y=\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac1{x+3/5}\right),\qquad -\frac35\lt x\lt \frac25,\qquad y\gt 0.\]
original.question_html:
\[y=\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac1{x+3/5}\right),\qquad -\frac35\lt x\lt \frac25,\qquad y\gt 0.\]
(a)[4]

Starting with \(\cosh y=1/(x+3/5)\), derive an expression for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).

(b)[6]

Find the first three terms of the Maclaurin expansion of \(y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Resolve the square root using the stated positive branch.

(b)

Differentiate the first derivative and divide its value by 2 for the x² term.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(v=x+3/5\). The stated domain gives \(0\lt v\lt 1\) and \(y\gt 0\). Differentiating the identity gives

\[\sinh y\,y^{\prime}=-v^{-2}.\]

Also \(\sinh y=\sqrt{\cosh^2y-1}=\sqrt{1-v^2}/v\) because \(v\gt 0\). Hence

\[y^{\prime}=- \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}} \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)}.\]

(b)

At zero, \(y(0)=\cosh^{-1}(5/3)=\ln3\). Differentiating the first derivative gives

\[y^{\prime\prime}=\frac{- \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right) \left(2 x + \frac{6}{5}\right) + 1}{\left(1 - \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}}.\]
\[y^{\prime}(0)=-\frac{25}{12},\qquad y^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac{875}{576}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{875 x^{2}}{1152} - \frac{25 x}{12} + \ln{\left(3 \right)}+O(x^3).\]

original.title: Logarithmic differentiation of an exponential base
original.question_html:
Let \(y=3^{2x}\).

(a)[3]

Differentiate \(\ln y\) to find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).

(b)[1]

(c)[3]

(b)

(c)

Since \(y\gt 0\), take logarithms: \(\ln y=2x\ln3\). Differentiate to obtain \(y^{\prime}/y=2\ln3\), hence \(y^{\prime}=2\ln3\,3^{2x}\).

\[y=2 x^{2} \ln{\left(3 \right)}^{2} + 2 x \ln{\left(3 \right)} + 1+O(x^3).\]

original.title: An implicit route to an inverse-hyperbolic series
original.stem_html:
The variables are related by

\[\tanh y=\cos(2x+\pi/3),\qquad -\frac\pi6\lt x\lt \frac\pi3.\]
original.question_html:
The variables are related by

\[\tanh y=\cos(2x+\pi/3),\qquad -\frac\pi6\lt x\lt \frac\pi3.\]
(a)[3]

Prove \(1-\tanh^2u=\operatorname{sech}^2u\) using exponential definitions.

(b)[4]

Differentiate implicitly and show that \(y^{\prime}=-2\operatorname{cosec}(2x+\pi/3)\).

(c)[5]

Find the first three terms of the Maclaurin series for \(y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the terms over the square of e^u+e^(−u).

(b)

Replace sech²y using the original relation before simplifying.

(c)

Remember the factor 1/2 in the quadratic Maclaurin term.
original.answer_html:
(a)

The identity follows from the exponential definitions.

(b)

\(- \frac{2}{\sin{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}}\).

(c)

\(\frac{4 x^{2}}{3} - \frac{4 \sqrt{3} x}{3} + \frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}\)\(+O(x^3)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

From the exponential definitions,

\[\tanh^2t+\operatorname{sech}^2t=\frac{(e^t-e^{-t})^2+4}{(e^t+e^{-t})^2}=\frac{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}{e^{2t}+2+e^{-2t}}=1.\]

Rearrange and rename the argument u.

(b)

\[\operatorname{sech}^2y\,y^{\prime}=-2\sin(2x+\pi/3).\]

By the identity and the original relation, \(\operatorname{sech}^2y=1-\cos^2(2x+\pi/3)=\sin^2(2x+\pi/3)\). The angle is strictly between 0 and π, so its sine is non-zero. Division gives the required result.

(c)

At x=0, tanh y=1/2, so \(y(0)=\tfrac12\ln3\). Part (b) gives \(y^{\prime}(0)=-4/\sqrt3\). Differentiate once more:

\[y^{\prime\prime}=4\operatorname{cosec}(2x+\pi/3)\cot(2x+\pi/3),\qquad y^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac83.\]

The quadratic coefficient is half the second derivative. Hence

\[y=\frac12\ln3-\frac4{\sqrt3}x+\frac43x^2+O(x^3).\]

Rearrange and rename the argument u.

parts.prompt_html: Find the first three terms of the Maclaurin series for \(y\).
parts.solution_html:
At x=0, tanh y=1/2, so \(y(0)=\tfrac12\ln3\). Part (b) gives \(y^{\prime}(0)=-4/\sqrt3\). Differentiate once more:

\[y^{\prime\prime}=4\operatorname{cosec}(2x+\pi/3)\cot(2x+\pi/3),\qquad y^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac83.\]

The quadratic coefficient is half the second derivative. Hence

\[y=\frac12\ln3-\frac4{\sqrt3}x+\frac43x^2+O(x^3).\]

original.title: An even hyperbolic expansion
original.stem_html:
Let

\[f(x)=\ln{\left(\cosh{\left(3 x \right)} \right)}.\]
original.question_html:
Let

\[f(x)=\ln{\left(\cosh{\left(3 x \right)} \right)}.\]
(a)[7]

By calculating derivatives at zero, find the Maclaurin expansion through the term in \(x^{4}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the value of f(0), including any logarithmic or exponential constant.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3+\frac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}x^4+O(x^{5}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=3 \tanh{\left(3 x \right)}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=\frac{9}{\cosh^{2}{\left(3 x \right)}}.\]
\[f^{(3)}(x)=- \frac{54 \sinh{\left(3 x \right)}}{\cosh^{3}{\left(3 x \right)}}.\]
\[f^{(4)}(x)=\frac{162 \left(\cosh{\left(6 x \right)} - 2\right)}{\cosh^{4}{\left(3 x \right)}}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=9,\qquad f^{(3)}(0)=0,\qquad f^{(4)}(0)=-162.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=- \frac{27 x^{4}}{4} + \frac{9 x^{2}}{2}+O(x^{5}).\]

original.title: A shifted tangent expansion
original.stem_html:
Let

\[f(x)=- \cot{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}.\]
original.question_html:
Let

\[f(x)=- \cot{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}.\]
(a)[5]

By calculating derivatives at zero, find the Maclaurin expansion through the term in \(x^{2}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the value of f(0), including any logarithmic or exponential constant.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Use the local Maclaurin formula

\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+O(x^{3}).\]
\[f^{(1)}(x)=\frac{2}{\sin^{2}{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}}.\]
\[f^{(2)}(x)=- \frac{8 \cot{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}}{\sin^{2}{\left(2 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}}.\]

The values at zero are

\[f^{(0)}(0)=- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3},\qquad f^{(1)}(0)=\frac{8}{3},\qquad f^{(2)}(0)=- \frac{32 \sqrt{3}}{9}.\]

Insert these values, dividing each derivative by its factorial:

\[f(x)=- \frac{16 \sqrt{3} x^{2}}{9} + \frac{8 x}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}+O(x^{3}).\]

original.title: A sparse expansion and what its coefficient means
original.stem_html:
Let

\[y=\sinh(2x^2)+\cosh(2x^2).\]
original.question_html:
Let

\[y=\sinh(2x^2)+\cosh(2x^2).\]
(a)[2]

Use a standard expansion to find the Maclaurin series through \(x^4\).

(b)[1]

Deduce \(y^{(4)}(0)\).

(c)[2]

Use the truncated series to approximate \(\int_0^{1/4}y\,dx\) as a rational fraction.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the two hyperbolic functions before expanding.

(b)

The coefficient is not itself the fourth derivative.

(c)

Integrate each retained term, then substitute 1/4.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The definitions give \(\sinh u+\cosh u=e^u\). Put \(u=2x^2\) in \(e^u=1+u+u^2/2+\cdots\):

\[y=1+2x^2+2x^4+O(x^6).\]

(b)

The coefficient of \(x^4\) is \(y^{(4)}(0)/4!\). Thus \(y^{(4)}(0)=2\times24=48\).

(c)

\[\int_0^{1/4}y\,dx\approx\left[x+\frac23x^3+\frac25x^5\right]_0^{1/4}=\frac{2003}{7680}.\]

The equality is with the integral of the polynomial, not with the exact integral of \(y\).

\[y=1+2x^2+2x^4+O(x^6).\]
